title: The Roof Puck
concept: Waymo posted on November 5th that it will run closed-course tests and collect heavy snowfall data in Alaska this season. The governor's post names Fairbanks, and a statement quoted by a TV station lists three kinds of work there, manual data collection, autonomous driving with a specialist at the wheel and limited structured testing. A Fairbanks resident asked whether the testers know to look for black ice. The film answers with Waymo's published design drawn as states of one roof sensor puck with a face, heated sensors and micro wipers, a stated backup sensing system in a whiteout, traction under each wheel, simulated black ice and a fleet that shares the weather, then gives the skeptics full strength on roadside billboards and concedes that the answer so far is on paper. Waymo's own post says service can pause for hours or days, the reports give no car count and no dates, the driverless question is unanswered, and the button leaves the puck half frosted on a vast dark road. This winter is the test.

fingerprint.light_story: ice-fog noon, whiteout, single lamp in the evening
fingerprint.metaphor: the roof sensor puck as the car's eye: every mechanism Waymo published is a state of that one smooth face against jagged rime, and the winter decides which state it ends in

palette: ice-fog noon, pink-gold low sun behind milky fog, ice-black ground, hoarfrost puck, plum ink on paper, sodium amber on live mechanisms only, a single crimson taillight
divergence_note: The last films were a true violet shore with a vermilion ticket machine and an acid lemon lamp (11-10), an oxblood courtroom (11-09), a permafrost road (11-08), a teal transformer yard (11-07) and a tangerine office (11-06); 11-02 keyed its whole cab in sodium amber. This film is a Fairbanks ice-fog noon, a pink-gold low sun behind milky fog over ice-black ground, with no lemon and no violet, amber only as emitted light on live mechanisms and never the key, and one deep crimson tail light, not vermilion. Its light arcs from low sun to whiteout white to one lamp at night. Its shape contrast is a smooth domed puck and soft rings against jagged rime and broken ice, its throughline is the puck's frost state, and it ends on a crane-up to one small car on a vast road, not an eye-level bookend.

treatment.title: The Roof Puck
treatment.summary: The residents' question is about seeing, and the thing that sees is the roof sensor puck, so the hero is the eye of the car with a face and the car stays a dark silhouette. Every mechanism Waymo published (heaters, micro wipers, stated backup sensing, traction under each wheel, simulated ice) is a state change on that one object, which makes the design legible without a single photoreal vehicle. The skeptics get their own roadside billboards at full strength, and the film concedes that every answer so far is on paper. The button leaves the puck half frosted on a vast dark road: the winter is the test.

angle.thesis: Fairbanks residents asked the right question, 'do they know to look for black ice', and Waymo's own published design answers it with a stack of specific mechanisms. What nobody has shown yet is whether that stack works at minus thirty, so the Fairbanks winter is the experiment, and the honest way to run it is exactly what Waymo's statement describes, slowly, with a specialist at the wheel.
angle.falsifier: False if the record shows the Fairbanks work is driverless public service (the statement says a specialist at the wheel, c13), or if Waymo's blog said nothing specific about ice (it names heaters, micro-wipers, traction under each wheel and simulated black ice, c17 to c20).

supporting_facts.fact: The blog says Alaska, the governor's post and KTUU say Fairbanks, and the company statement lists three kinds of work.
The published design has an answer to each of the residents' worries, heated sensors, redundant sensing, per-wheel traction and simulated ice.
The test described is cautious by construction, a specialist at the wheel, limited structured testing, and unanswered questions about driverless plans.

angle.fair_counterpoint: Residents' worry is not naive. Howe asks whether the testers know black ice, Jackson expects stalls at minus thirty. A design page is a claim, not a result, and the same blog says service can pause for hours or days when weather passes what the system is validated for. Nothing in the reports says how many cars, what dates, or whether driverless service is intended.
angle.valence: curious, leaning hopeful. Alaska as the place where an AI driver gets its hardest winter exam, with the residents' skepticism treated as the exam's first question.

second_movement.recontextualizing_fact: c22 and c23. Each Waymo car is a mobile weather station, sharing what it sees across the fleet, so a winter spent in Fairbanks isn't one car learning, it is the whole fleet learning. And c24 says the other side of that, the company will pause service for hours or days when the weather beats its validation.
second_movement.test: Draw the skeptics at full strength as their own scene. Howe's black ice question, Jackson's stalled car at minus thirty, Woolwine's no. Then let the film narrow honestly. The design page answers the question on paper, the test exists because paper isn't enough, and the reports don't say how many cars or when.

hook.frame1: A mittened hand wipes a frosted window, a headlight sweeps a dry-looking road and it turns into a mirror holding a frosted roof puck upside down.
hook.headline: DO THEY KNOW BLACK ICE?
hook.loopback: The button returns to a road at night under one lamp, the question-mark frost creeping back over the puck, and rises away to one small car reflected upside down in black ice, the mirror of frame one.

open_loop.what: How many cars, and when? Planted as a quiet blank odometer rolling in the corner of the phone with its own tick and a 0.4 s glow, paid when the same counter and a new blank calendar hold empty on the specialist's clipboard, NO COUNT, NO DATES.

open_loop_2.what: What does the system do when winter wins? Planted when the backup returns draw the road as dots thinning toward a dashed white wall, paid on the same dot road as the rings shrink, the car eases to the shoulder with hazards blinking and calendar leaves stack like snow, PAUSE FOR HOURS OR DAYS.
